doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

chapter: Jazz players and the record industry
title: Old labels, talent and home studios
summary: John Hammond's talent finds, talented hip hop kids, and the pros and cons of home recording.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Big time. Big time. And then it seems like one of the great things about the old record labels was they were really looking for — like I read an article recently about John Hammond, who I never knew was related to the Vanderbilts you know. I mean I had known his son, who was a great guitar player John Hammond Jr. In the '60s I met him. But I mean John Hammond, if you list the names of the people that he found and that recorded, they were all brilliant. They were so talented. It doesn't seem like you could make a living in those days unless you were pretty good.
I'm going to quote you on that. That's a good one.

You know well I don't know whether it's true, sir but I definitely have a feeling like that. It's like even among the hip hop community there were some kids that were so overtly talented that you knew they were going to do well when I met them as kids. Because they were like open books. They were like jazz musicians in their own way. They really loved music, they loved assembly, they loved putting things together, they liked the rhythm of the whole event. And yeah I mean in one way it's really good, the fact that people can make records in their house because it's more creative for the people but then it's less creative because then there's a lot less people playing and learning instruments. And I mean I don't know where this balance goes and I don't know —
